Q01. What is the Spring Framework?

📝 Topic Focus: 1. What is the Spring Framework?

1. What is the Spring Framework?

Spring Framework is an open-source, lightweight Java framework used to develop enterprise-level applications. It simplifies Java development by providing features like Dependency Injection (DI), Inversion of Control (IoC), transaction management and database connectivity.

Main Features

  1. Lightweight: Requires fewer resources and simplifies application development.
  2. IoC (Inversion of Control): Spring manages the creation and lifecycle of objects.
  3. DI (Dependency Injection): Automatically provides required dependencies to objects.
  4. AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming): Handles common tasks like logging and security.
  5. Transaction Management: Simplifies database transaction handling.
  6. Spring MVC: Helps develop web applications.
  7. Database Integration: Supports JDBC, Hibernate and JPA.

Spring Framework Architecture

🔍 Spring Framework Architecture (Core Container, AOP, Data Access, Web, Test) (tap to expand)

Example

@Component
class Student {
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Student Details");
    }
}

Here, @Component tells Spring to manage the Student class as a Spring Bean.

Advantages

  • Reduces boilerplate code.
  • Makes applications loosely coupled.
  • Improves code reusability.
  • Simplifies testing and maintenance.

Easy Memory Trick

Remember I-D-A-T-M:

  • I – Inversion of Control
  • D – Dependency Injection
  • A – Aspect-Oriented Programming
  • T – Transaction Management
  • M – MVC

Important: Spring Framework is mainly known for IoC and Dependency Injection.

Q02. What is the use of @ComponentScan?

📝 Topic Focus: 2. What is the use of @ComponentScan?

2. What is the use of @ComponentScan?

@ComponentScan is an annotation in the Spring Framework used to automatically scan specified packages to identify classes annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller.

It registers the detected classes as Spring Beans in the Spring IoC Container. This helps Spring manage objects automatically without requiring manual bean configuration.

Uses of @ComponentScan

  1. Automatic Component Detection: It searches specified packages for classes containing Spring annotations.

  2. Bean Registration: It automatically registers detected classes as Spring Beans.

  3. Reduces Manual Configuration: Developers do not need to manually define every bean in the configuration class.

  4. Package Scanning: It allows developers to specify which packages Spring should scan.

Example

@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.example")
public class AppConfig {
}

Explanation: - @Configuration indicates that the class contains Spring configuration. - @ComponentScan enables package scanning. - basePackages = "com.example" specifies the package that Spring should scan.

Suppose we have the following class:

@Component
public class Student {
    public void display() {
        System.out.println("Student Details");
    }
}

Spring automatically detects the Student class and registers it as a Spring Bean.

Conclusion

@ComponentScan simplifies Spring application configuration by automatically detecting and registering annotated classes as Spring Beans.

Important: It is mainly used for automatic component scanning and bean registration.

Q03. What is Autowiring in Spring?

📝 Topic Focus: 3. What is Auto Wiring in Spring?

3. What is Autowiring in Spring?

Autowiring in Spring is a feature that automatically injects the required dependencies (objects) into a class without manually creating or configuring them.

It is a part of Dependency Injection (DI) and helps reduce manual coding and makes applications loosely coupled.

Types of Autowiring

Spring supports different types of dependency injection:

  1. Constructor Injection: Dependencies are provided through the class constructor.

  2. Setter Injection: Dependencies are provided using setter methods.

  3. Field Injection: Dependencies are directly injected into class variables using @Autowired.

@Autowired Annotation

Spring uses the @Autowired annotation to automatically inject dependencies.

Example:

@Component
class Student {
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Student Details");
    }
}

@Component
class College {

    @Autowired
    Student student;

    void show() {
        student.display();
    }
}

Explanation:

  • @Component tells Spring to manage the classes as Spring Beans.
  • @Autowired tells Spring to inject the required Student object into the College class.
  • Spring automatically manages the dependency through its IoC Container.

Advantages of Autowiring

  1. Reduces manual object creation.
  2. Simplifies dependency management.
  3. Reduces boilerplate code.
  4. Promotes loose coupling.
  5. Improves code maintainability.

Conclusion: Autowiring simplifies dependency injection by allowing Spring to automatically provide the required objects to a class.

Important: The @Autowired annotation is commonly used for automatic dependency injection in Spring.

Q04. Name any Four Spring Bean Scopes

📝 Topic Focus: 4. Name any four Spring Bean scopes

4. Name any Four Spring Bean Scopes

Spring Bean Scopes define the lifecycle and visibility of a Spring Bean, specifying how many instances Spring creates and how long they remain available.

The four Spring Bean scopes are:

  1. Singleton Scope:
  2. Only one instance of a bean is created per Spring IoC Container.

  3. It is the default scope in Spring.

  4. Prototype Scope:

  5. A new bean instance is created every time it is requested from the container.

  6. Request Scope:

  7. A new bean instance is created for each HTTP request.

  8. It is used in web applications.

  9. Session Scope:

  10. A single bean instance is created for each HTTP session.
  11. It remains available throughout that session.

Example

@Component
@Scope("prototype")
public class Student {
}

Here, @Scope("prototype") tells Spring to create a new Student bean instance whenever it is requested from the container.

Note: Spring also supports other scopes, such as Application and WebSocket scopes.

Easy Memory Trick: S-P-R-S = Singleton, Prototype, Request, Session.

Q05. Differentiate Between Query Methods and Named Queries

📝 Topic Focus: 5. Differentiate between Query Methods and Named Queries

5. Differentiate Between Query Methods and Named Queries

In Spring Data JPA, Query Methods and Named Queries are two ways to retrieve data from a database. Both are used to perform database operations, but they differ in how queries are defined and executed.

Difference Between Query Methods and Named Queries

Query Methods Named Queries
1. Queries are created using method names. Queries are defined with a specific name.
2. Follow predefined naming conventions. Use JPQL or SQL query definitions.
3. Written directly in the Repository interface. Usually defined using @NamedQuery or @NamedNativeQuery.
4. Suitable for simple queries. Suitable for more complex queries.
5. Require less coding. Require separate query definitions.
6. Spring Data JPA derives the query from the method name. The application refers to the predefined query by its name.

1. Query Methods Example

public interface StudentRepository
       extends JpaRepository<Student, Integer> {

    List<Student> findByName(String name);
}

Here, Spring Data JPA automatically generates a query based on the method name findByName().

2. Named Queries Example

@Entity
@NamedQuery(
    name = "Student.findAllStudents",
    query = "SELECT s FROM Student s"
)
public class Student {
    @Id
    private int id;
}

Repository method:

List<Student> findAllStudents();

Here, the query is defined separately using @NamedQuery and can be referenced by its name.

Conclusion: Query Methods are best for simple database queries, whereas Named Queries are useful when queries need to be predefined and reused.

Easy Memory Trick: - Query Methods = Query from Method Name. - Named Queries = Predefined Query with a Name.

Q06. What is Pagination in Spring Data JPA?

📝 Topic Focus: 6. What is Pagination in Spring Data JPA?

6. What is Pagination in Spring Data JPA?

Pagination in Spring Data JPA is a technique used to divide a large amount of database records into smaller pages. Instead of retrieving all records at once, it fetches a limited number of records per page.

It improves application performance and reduces memory usage, especially when working with large datasets.

Main Features of Pagination

  1. Pageable: An interface used to define the page number and page size.
  2. PageRequest: A class used to create pagination requests.
  3. Page: An interface that contains the requested records and information about the total pages and records.
  4. Sorting: Pagination can also be combined with sorting to arrange records.

Example

public interface StudentRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Student, Integer> {
}

Using Pagination:

Pageable pageable = PageRequest.of(0, 5);

Page<Student> students =
    studentRepository.findAll(pageable);

Explanation

  • PageRequest.of(0, 5) creates a request for the first page containing 5 records.
  • findAll(pageable) retrieves the requested records.
  • Page<Student> stores the result and pagination details.

Example:

Suppose a database contains 100 student records and the page size is 10.

  • Page 1: Records 1–10
  • Page 2: Records 11–20
  • Page 3: Records 21–30
  • Page 10: Records 91–100

Advantages

  1. Reduces unnecessary data retrieval.
  2. Improves application performance.
  3. Reduces memory consumption.
  4. Makes large datasets easier to display.

Conclusion: Pagination helps retrieve database records in smaller pages using Pageable, PageRequest, and Page in Spring Data JPA.

Q07. State Any Two Advantages of Web Services

📝 Topic Focus: 7. State any two advantages of Web Services

7. State Any Two Advantages of Web Services

Web Services are software components that allow different applications to communicate and exchange data over a network using standard protocols such as HTTP. They help applications developed using different programming languages and platforms work together.

Two Advantages of Web Services

1. Platform Independence

  • Web Services can work on different operating systems and platforms.
  • They allow applications developed using different programming languages to communicate.
  • They do not depend on a specific operating system or programming language.
  • Example: A Java application running on Windows can communicate with a Python application running on Linux using a Web Service.

2. Reusability

  • Web Services allow the same functionality to be used by multiple applications.
  • Developers do not need to write the same code repeatedly.
  • A single Web Service can be accessed by different applications whenever required.
  • Example: An online payment service can be reused by multiple shopping applications for processing payments.

Other Advantages of Web Services

Although the question asks for only two advantages, some other important advantages are:

  1. Interoperability: Different applications can communicate with each other.
  2. Loose Coupling: Applications can interact without depending heavily on each other's internal implementation.
  3. Easy Integration: Web Services make it easier to connect different software systems.

Conclusion

Web Services make communication between different applications easier. Platform Independence and Reusability are two major advantages that help developers build flexible and reusable software applications.

Important Exam Points: Platform Independence and Reusability are the two main advantages asked in this question.

Q08. What is the Purpose of the HTTP GET Method in REST?

📝 Topic Focus: 8. What is the purpose of the HTTP GET method in REST?

8. What is the Purpose of the HTTP GET Method in REST?

The HTTP GET method in REST (Representational State Transfer) is used to retrieve or fetch data from a server. It allows clients to request specific resources without modifying or deleting the data stored on the server.

It is one of the commonly used HTTP methods in RESTful Web Services.

Main Purposes of HTTP GET

  1. Retrieve Data: It fetches information from the server, such as student details, product information or user records.

  2. Access Resources: It allows clients to access specific resources using a URL.

  3. Read Operations: It is mainly used for reading data without changing the server's state.

  4. Query Parameters: It supports query parameters to filter or search for specific information.

Example

Suppose a student management application needs to retrieve student details.

HTTP Request:

GET /api/students/101 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

Response:

{
  "id": 101,
  "name": "Rahul",
  "course": "AI and ML"
}

Important Characteristics

  • Safe Method: GET does not modify the server's data.
  • Idempotent: Repeating the same GET request produces the same intended effect.
  • Cacheable: GET responses can be cached to improve performance.
  • No Request Body Required: GET requests generally use URL parameters to send filtering information.

Conclusion

The main purpose of the HTTP GET method in REST is to retrieve resources from a server without modifying the existing data.

Important: GET = Retrieve or Read Data.

Q09. What is Exception Handling in Spring REST?

📝 Topic Focus: 9. What is Exception Handling in Spring REST?

9. What is Exception Handling in Spring REST?

Exception Handling in Spring REST is a mechanism used to handle errors and exceptions that occur while processing REST API requests. It prevents the application from crashing and provides meaningful error responses to clients.

Spring provides annotations such as @ExceptionHandler, @ControllerAdvice, and @RestControllerAdvice to manage exceptions.

Main Annotations Used

  1. @ExceptionHandler: Used to handle specific exceptions within a controller.
  2. @ControllerAdvice: Provides global exception handling across multiple controllers.
  3. @RestControllerAdvice: Combines @ControllerAdvice and @ResponseBody to return error responses directly in the response body.

Example

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    public ResponseEntity<String> handleException(
            Exception ex) {

        return ResponseEntity
            .status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
            .body("Something went wrong");
    }
}

Explanation

  • @RestControllerAdvice enables global exception handling.
  • @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) handles exceptions of type Exception.
  • ResponseEntity is used to return the HTTP status code and error message.
  • INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR represents HTTP status code 500.

Advantages of Exception Handling

  1. Prevents Application Failure: Handles unexpected errors properly.
  2. Meaningful Error Messages: Provides understandable error information to clients.
  3. Centralized Handling: Manages exceptions from multiple controllers in one place.
  4. Better API Response: Returns appropriate HTTP status codes such as 400, 404 and 500.

Conclusion: Exception Handling in Spring REST helps manage application errors and return proper HTTP error responses to clients.

Q10. What is Meant by Securing a REST Endpoint?

📝 Topic Focus: 10. What is meant by securing a REST endpoint?

10. What is Meant by Securing a REST Endpoint?

Securing a REST Endpoint means protecting a REST API URL from unauthorized access and ensuring that only authenticated and authorized users can access specific resources or perform operations.

It helps protect sensitive data and prevents unauthorized users from accessing or modifying application information.

Main Methods of Securing REST Endpoints

  1. Authentication: Verifies the identity of a user before allowing access. Example: Username and password login.

  2. Authorization: Determines what an authenticated user is allowed to access or perform. Example: Only an admin can delete student records.

  3. HTTPS: Uses encrypted communication between the client and server to protect data from being intercepted.

  4. Token-Based Authentication: Uses tokens such as JWT (JSON Web Token) to verify users when they send API requests.

  5. Role-Based Access Control: Provides permissions based on user roles such as Admin, Teacher and Student.

Example

Consider a Student Management REST API.

GET /api/students
Authorization: Bearer <token>

Explanation: - The client sends a request to access student details. - The server checks the authentication token. - If the token is valid and the user has permission, access is granted. - Otherwise, the server returns an appropriate error response.

Common HTTP Status Codes

Status Code Meaning
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
200 Successful Request

Importance

  • Protects sensitive information.
  • Prevents unauthorized access.
  • Ensures secure communication.
  • Controls user permissions.

Conclusion: Securing a REST endpoint ensures that API resources are accessed only by authorized users through authentication, authorization and secure communication.

Q11. Define Spring Framework.

📝 Topic Focus: 11. Define Spring Framework.

11. Define Spring Framework.

Spring Framework is an open-source, lightweight Java framework used to develop enterprise-level applications. It simplifies Java application development by providing features such as Inversion of Control (IoC), Dependency Injection (DI), Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP), transaction management and database connectivity.

It helps developers build applications that are loosely coupled, reusable, maintainable and easier to test.

Main Features of Spring Framework

  1. Lightweight: Spring provides a lightweight infrastructure for developing Java applications.

  2. Inversion of Control (IoC): Spring manages the creation and lifecycle of objects instead of developers managing them manually.

  3. Dependency Injection (DI): Automatically provides the required dependencies to objects.

  4. Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP): Separates common tasks such as logging, security and transaction management from business logic.

  5. Transaction Management: Provides support for managing database transactions.

  6. Spring MVC: Supports the development of web applications using the Model-View-Controller architecture.

  7. Database Integration: Supports technologies such as JDBC, Hibernate and JPA.

Example

@Component
public class Student {
    public void display() {
        System.out.println("Hello Student");
    }
}

Here, @Component tells Spring to manage the Student class as a Spring Bean.

Conclusion

Spring Framework simplifies Java application development by providing built-in features for object management, dependency injection, database operations and web development.

Important Exam Point: Spring Framework is mainly known for IoC and Dependency Injection, which help create loosely coupled applications.

Q13. What is IoC (Inversion of Control)?

📝 Topic Focus: 13. What is IoC (Inversion of Control)?

13. What is IoC (Inversion of Control)?

IoC (Inversion of Control) is a design principle in the Spring Framework in which the control of creating, managing and configuring objects is transferred from the programmer to the Spring Container.

Normally, developers create objects manually using the new keyword. But with IoC, Spring manages object creation and their lifecycle automatically.

Working of IoC

  1. The developer creates Java classes and defines their dependencies.
  2. Spring Container scans or reads the configuration.
  3. It creates the required objects (Spring Beans).
  4. It manages their lifecycle.
  5. It injects dependencies wherever required.

Example

Without IoC:

class Student {
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Student Details");
    }
}

class College {
    Student s = new Student();
}

Here, the developer manually creates the Student object using the new keyword.

With IoC:

@Component
class Student {
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Student Details");
    }
}

@Component
class College {
    @Autowired
    Student student;
}

Here, Spring automatically creates and injects the Student object into the College class.

Advantages of IoC

  1. Loose Coupling: Reduces dependency between classes.
  2. Easy Maintenance: Makes applications easier to modify.
  3. Reusability: Allows objects to be reused.
  4. Easy Testing: Makes unit testing easier.

Conclusion

IoC transfers object creation and management responsibility from the developer to the Spring Container.

Important: IoC is the main principle behind Dependency Injection (DI) in Spring.

Q14. Define Dependency Injection (DI).

📝 Topic Focus: 14. Define Dependency Injection.

14. Define Dependency Injection (DI).

Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern in the Spring Framework in which the required objects (dependencies) are provided to a class by the Spring Container instead of the class creating those objects manually.

It is a method of implementing Inversion of Control (IoC). DI helps create loosely coupled applications and makes code easier to maintain and test.

Types of Dependency Injection

Spring supports three main types of Dependency Injection:

  1. Constructor Injection: Dependencies are provided through the class constructor.

  2. Setter Injection: Dependencies are provided using setter methods.

  3. Field Injection: Dependencies are directly injected into class variables using the @Autowired annotation.

Example

@Component
class Student {
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Student Details");
    }
}

@Component
class College {

    @Autowired
    Student student;
}

Explanation

  • @Component tells Spring to manage the classes as Spring Beans.
  • @Autowired tells Spring to inject the required Student object into the College class.
  • Spring Container automatically manages the dependency.

Advantages of Dependency Injection

  1. Loose Coupling: Reduces dependency between classes.
  2. Code Reusability: Allows objects to be reused.
  3. Easy Testing: Makes unit testing easier.
  4. Easy Maintenance: Makes applications easier to modify and manage.

Conclusion

Dependency Injection simplifies object management by allowing Spring to provide the required dependencies automatically instead of creating objects manually.

Important: DI is a way to achieve IoC in the Spring Framework.

Q16. Explain the Concept of Auto Scanning with Annotations and How It Works.

16. Explain the Concept of Auto Scanning with Annotations and How It Works.

Auto Scanning in the Spring Framework is a feature that automatically detects classes annotated with Spring annotations and registers them as Spring Beans in the IoC Container. It reduces manual configuration and makes application development easier.

Spring uses the @ComponentScan annotation to scan specified packages and identify classes that need to be managed by the Spring Container.

Important Annotations Used in Auto Scanning

  1. @Component: Marks a Java class as a Spring-managed component.
  2. @Service: Identifies a class that contains business logic.
  3. @Repository: Identifies a class responsible for database operations.
  4. @Controller: Identifies a class that handles web requests.
  5. @RestController: Identifies a class that handles REST API requests and returns data directly.
  6. @ComponentScan: Tells Spring which packages to scan for annotated classes.

How Auto Scanning Works

Auto Scanning works through the following steps:

  1. Define Components: Developers add annotations such as @Component, @Service or @Repository to Java classes.
  2. Enable Component Scanning: The @ComponentScan annotation specifies the packages to scan.
  3. Scan Packages: Spring searches the specified packages for annotated classes.
  4. Register Beans: Spring automatically registers the detected classes as Spring Beans.
  5. Dependency Injection: Spring injects the required dependencies using annotations such as @Autowired.

Example

@Component
public class Student {
    public void display() {
        System.out.println("Student Details");
    }
}

Configuration Class:

@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.example")
public class AppConfig {
}

Explanation

  • @Component marks the Student class as a Spring component.
  • @Configuration defines the configuration class.
  • @ComponentScan instructs Spring to scan the com.example package.
  • Spring detects the Student class and registers it as a Bean.

Advantages of Auto Scanning

  1. Reduces manual bean configuration.
  2. Simplifies application development.
  3. Supports automatic dependency management.
  4. Improves code organization and maintainability.

Conclusion: Auto Scanning automatically detects and registers Spring components as Beans using annotations and @ComponentScan, reducing manual configuration in Spring applications.

Q17. Explain IoC Container Using Java-Based Configuration.

📝 Topic Focus: Explain IoC container using Java-based configuration.

17. Explain IoC Container Using Java-Based Configuration.

IoC (Inversion of Control) Container is the core part of the Spring Framework that manages the creation, configuration and lifecycle of objects called Spring Beans. Instead of creating and managing objects manually, developers allow the Spring Container to handle these responsibilities.

In Java-Based Configuration, Spring uses Java classes and annotations to configure beans instead of XML configuration files.

Main Annotations Used

  1. @Configuration: Indicates that a Java class contains Spring bean configuration.
  2. @Bean: Defines a method whose returned object is registered as a Spring Bean.
  3. @Autowired: Automatically injects required dependencies.
  4. @ComponentScan: Scans specified packages to detect Spring components.

Working of IoC Container

  1. The developer creates a Java configuration class.
  2. The @Configuration annotation identifies the configuration class.
  3. The @Bean annotation defines the objects managed by Spring.
  4. Spring Container reads the configuration and creates the required beans.
  5. It manages bean dependencies and their lifecycle.
  6. The application retrieves the required beans from the container.

Example

Step 1: Create a Java Class

public class Student {
    public void display() {
        System.out.println("Student Details");
    }
}

Step 2: Create Configuration Class

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public Student student() {
        return new Student();
    }
}

Step 3: Access Bean Using IoC Container

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        ApplicationContext context =
            new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(
                AppConfig.class);

        Student s = context.getBean(Student.class);

        s.display();
    }
}

Explanation

  • @Configuration defines the configuration class.
  • @Bean registers the Student object in the Spring Container.
  • AnnotationConfigApplicationContext creates the IoC Container using Java configuration.
  • getBean() retrieves the Student object from the container.
  • display() executes the method.

Advantages

  1. Reduces manual object creation.
  2. Avoids XML configuration.
  3. Supports Dependency Injection.
  4. Improves code maintainability.
  5. Makes application configuration easier.

Conclusion: Java-Based Configuration allows the Spring IoC Container to manage beans using Java classes and annotations instead of XML files.

Q18. Differentiate Between Constructor Injection and Setter Injection

📝 Topic Focus: Differentiate between Constructor Injection and Setter Injection

18. Differentiate Between Constructor Injection and Setter Injection

Constructor Injection and Setter Injection are two types of Dependency Injection (DI) in the Spring Framework. Both are used to provide required dependencies to a class, but they differ in how dependencies are supplied.

Difference Between Constructor Injection and Setter Injection

Constructor Injection Setter Injection
1. Dependencies are provided through a class constructor. Dependencies are provided through setter methods.
2. Uses a constructor to inject dependencies. Uses setter methods to inject dependencies.
3. Dependencies are provided when the object is created. Dependencies can be provided after the object is created.
4. Suitable for mandatory dependencies. Suitable for optional dependencies.
5. Makes dependencies immutable when final fields are used. Dependencies can be changed after object creation.
6. Helps ensure that required dependencies are available during object creation. Allows dependencies to be set or changed later.
7. Generally preferred for required dependencies. Useful when dependencies are optional or need modification.

1. Constructor Injection Example

@Component
class Student {
    private final Address address;

    @Autowired
    Student(Address address) {
        this.address = address;
    }
}

Explanation: Spring provides the Address object through the constructor when creating the Student object.

2. Setter Injection Example

@Component
class Student {
    private Address address;

    @Autowired
    public void setAddress(Address address) {
        this.address = address;
    }
}

Explanation: Spring provides the Address object through the setter method after creating the Student object.

Advantages

Constructor Injection: - Ensures required dependencies are provided. - Supports immutable objects. - Makes unit testing easier.

Setter Injection: - Supports optional dependencies. - Allows dependency changes after object creation. - Useful for flexible configuration.

Conclusion

Constructor Injection is preferred for mandatory dependencies, whereas Setter Injection is suitable for optional dependencies that may need to be changed later.

Easy Memory Trick: - Constructor = Dependency through Constructor. - Setter = Dependency through Setter Method.

Q21. What is @SpringBootApplication Annotation?

@SpringBootApplication is a special annotation in the Spring Boot Framework used to mark the main class of a Spring Boot application. It enables automatic configuration, component scanning and configuration support.

It simplifies application setup by combining three important Spring annotations into a single annotation.

Three Main Annotations

  1. @SpringBootConfiguration:
  2. Indicates that the class provides configuration for the Spring Boot application.

  3. It is a specialized form of @Configuration.

  4. @EnableAutoConfiguration:

  4. Simplifies Spring Boot application startup.

Q22. Describe How Autowiring Works Internally in Spring.

📝 Topic Focus: 22. Describe how Auto Wiring works internally in Spring

22. Describe How Autowiring Works Internally in Spring.

Autowiring in Spring is a feature of Dependency Injection (DI) that automatically provides the required dependencies to a class without manually creating objects. Spring uses the @Autowired annotation to identify where dependencies need to be injected.

Internal Working of Autowiring

Autowiring works internally through the following steps:

  1. Bean Creation: Spring IoC Container starts creating objects (Spring Beans) based on configuration and component scanning.

  2. Dependency Detection: Spring detects the @Autowired annotation in constructors, fields or setter methods.

  3. Dependency Search: Spring searches the IoC Container for a suitable bean that matches the required dependency type.

  4. Bean Matching: Spring checks the available beans to find a matching dependency. If multiple beans of the same type exist, it can use @Qualifier to identify the correct bean.

  5. Dependency Injection: Spring injects the matching bean into the required class.

  6. Bean Initialization: After dependency injection, Spring completes bean initialization and makes the object available for application use.

Example

@Component
class Student {
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Student Details");
    }
}

@Component
class College {

    @Autowired
    private Student student;

    void show() {
        student.display();
    }
}

Explanation

  • @Component registers both classes as Spring Beans.
  • @Autowired tells Spring to inject the Student dependency into College.
  • Spring searches the IoC Container for a matching Student bean.
  • It injects the dependency automatically.
  • The show() method uses the injected object.

Important Points

  1. Autowiring reduces manual object creation.
  2. It supports constructor, setter and field injection.
  3. It helps achieve loose coupling.
  4. If multiple matching beans exist, @Qualifier can specify the required bean.
  5. If no matching bean is found for a required dependency, Spring generally throws an error.

Conclusion

Autowiring internally works by detecting dependencies, searching for matching Spring Beans and injecting them into the required classes through the IoC Container.

Q24. Explain Different Bean Scopes in Spring and Describe the Use of Loggers with Suitable Examples.

📝 Topic Focus: 24. Explain different bean scopes in Spring and describe the use of loggers with suitable examples.

24. Explain Different Bean Scopes in Spring and Describe the Use of Loggers with Suitable Examples.

1. Bean Scopes in Spring

Bean Scope defines the lifecycle and visibility of a Spring Bean. It determines how many instances of a bean Spring creates and how long those instances remain available.

Spring supports the following bean scopes:

  1. Singleton: Only one instance of a bean is created per Spring IoC Container. It is the default scope.

  2. Prototype: A new bean instance is created every time the bean is requested from the container.

  3. Request: A new bean instance is created for each HTTP request. It is used in web applications.

  4. Session: One bean instance is created for each HTTP session and remains available throughout that session.

  5. Application: One bean instance is created per ServletContext and shared across the web application.

  6. WebSocket: A separate bean instance is created for each WebSocket session.

Example:

@Component
@Scope("prototype")
public class Student {
}

Here, Spring creates a new Student bean whenever it is requested from the container.

2. Loggers in Spring

Logger is a tool used to record application activities, events, warnings and errors during program execution.

Spring Boot commonly uses SLF4J as a logging API with Logback as its default logging implementation.

Uses of Loggers

  1. Debugging: Helps identify errors in the application.
  2. Monitoring: Tracks application activities.
  3. Error Tracking: Records exceptions and failures.
  4. Information Recording: Displays important application events.

Logger Example

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

@RestController
public class StudentController {

    private static final Logger logger =
        LoggerFactory.getLogger(StudentController.class);

    @GetMapping("/student")
    public String getStudent() {

        logger.info("Student API called");

        return "Student Details";
    }
}

Explanation: - LoggerFactory creates a logger. - logger.info() records an informational message. - The message appears in the application logs when the API is called.

Conclusion

Bean scopes control the lifecycle and number of Spring Bean instances, while loggers help monitor application activities and identify errors during execution.

Q25. Describe the Role of Logback in Spring Boot.

25. Describe the Role of Logback in Spring Boot.

Logback is a logging framework used in Spring Boot to record application activities, events, warnings and errors during program execution. It is the default logging implementation used by Spring Boot when the standard logging starter is included.

Logback helps developers monitor applications, identify errors and understand application behaviour.

Main Roles of Logback in Spring Boot

  1. Application Monitoring: Records important application activities, such as application startup and API requests.

  2. Error Tracking: Records errors and exceptions to help developers identify and fix problems.

  3. Different Logging Levels: Supports different logging levels to classify messages according to their importance.

  4. File Logging: Stores log messages in files for future reference and analysis.

  5. Log Formatting: Controls how log messages are displayed using patterns.

  6. Configuration: Allows developers to configure logging through files such as logback-spring.xml.

Logging Levels in Logback

Level Purpose
TRACE Records very detailed information.
DEBUG Provides debugging information.
INFO Records normal application activities.
WARN Indicates potential problems.
ERROR Records serious errors.

Example

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

@RestController
public class StudentController {

    private static final Logger logger =
        LoggerFactory.getLogger(StudentController.class);

        logger.info("Student API called");
        logger.warn("Warning message");
        logger.error("Error occurred");

        return "Student Details";
    }
}

Explanation

  • LoggerFactory creates a logger for the class.
  • logger.info() records informational messages.
  • logger.warn() records warning messages.
  • logger.error() records error messages.
  • Logback processes and displays these messages according to the logging configuration.

Advantages of Logback

  2. Supports multiple logging levels.

Q26. Explain the Concept of AOP and Its Benefits.

📝 Topic Focus: 26. Explain the concept of AOP and its benefits.

26. Explain the Concept of AOP and Its Benefits.

AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming) is a programming approach used in the Spring Framework to separate common tasks from the main business logic of an application.

These common tasks are called Cross-Cutting Concerns, such as logging, security, transaction management and exception handling.

AOP helps developers manage these tasks separately without repeatedly writing the same code in different classes.

Important Terminologies of AOP

  1. Aspect: A class that contains common functionality, such as logging or security.
  2. Join Point: A point during program execution where an aspect can be applied, such as a method execution.
  3. Advice: The action performed by an aspect at a particular join point.
  4. Pointcut: An expression that identifies where advice should be executed.
  5. Weaving: The process of connecting aspects with the application code.

Types of Advice

  1. Before Advice: Executes before a method.
  2. After Advice: Executes after a method completes.
  3. After Returning: Executes when a method completes successfully.
  4. After Throwing: Executes when a method throws an exception.
  5. Around Advice: Executes before and after a method.

Example

@Aspect
@Component
public class LoggingAspect {

    @Before("execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))")
    public void logBefore() {
        System.out.println("Method is executing");
    }
}

Explanation: - @Aspect defines the class as an aspect. - @Component registers it as a Spring Bean. - @Before executes advice before the matching method. - execution() defines which methods should be intercepted.

Benefits of AOP

  1. Code Reusability: Common functionality can be reused.
  2. Loose Coupling: Separates business logic from common tasks.
  3. Easy Maintenance: Changes to common functionality can be made centrally.
  4. Better Readability: Keeps business logic clean and simple.
  5. Reduced Code Duplication: Avoids repeating logging and security code.

Conclusion

AOP separates cross-cutting concerns from business logic, making Spring applications more modular, reusable and maintainable.

Q28. What Are the Major Limitations of the JDBC API? Why Is Spring Data JPA Preferred Over Traditional JDBC?

📝 Topic Focus: 28. What are the major limitations of the JDBC API? Why is Spring Data JPA preferred over traditional JDBC?

28. What Are the Major Limitations of the JDBC API? Why Is Spring Data JPA Preferred Over Traditional JDBC?

JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) is a Java API used to connect Java applications with databases and perform operations such as INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT.

However, traditional JDBC requires developers to write more code and manage database operations manually. Spring Data JPA provides a simpler approach using ORM and repository-based operations.

1. Major Limitations of JDBC API

  1. Boilerplate Code: Developers must write lengthy code for database connections, statements and result processing.

  2. Manual Resource Management: Connections, statements and result sets must be closed manually to avoid resource leaks.

  3. SQL Dependency: Developers need to write SQL queries manually for database operations.

  4. Exception Handling: JDBC requires handling SQLException explicitly.

  5. Object Mapping: Developers must manually convert database records into Java objects.

  6. Difficult Maintenance: Large applications become difficult to maintain because of repeated database code.

2. Why Spring Data JPA Is Preferred Over JDBC

Spring Data JPA simplifies database operations by providing repository interfaces and automatic query generation.

Example:

public interface EmployeeRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Employee, Integer> {

    List<Employee> findByName(String name);
}

Here, Spring Data JPA automatically generates the required query from the method name.

3. Difference Between JDBC and Spring Data JPA

JDBC Spring Data JPA
Requires manual SQL queries. Supports automatic query generation.
Requires more boilerplate code. Reduces boilerplate code.
Manual object mapping. Supports automatic ORM mapping.
Manual resource management. Provides simplified resource management.
Requires explicit SQL exception handling. Uses Spring's exception translation.

4. Advantages of Spring Data JPA

  1. Reduces database-related coding.
  2. Simplifies CRUD operations.
  3. Supports pagination and sorting.
  4. Improves code reusability.
  5. Makes database application development easier.

Conclusion

Spring Data JPA is preferred over traditional JDBC because it reduces coding complexity, provides automatic object mapping and simplifies database operations.

Q29. Compare Derived Query Methods, @Query, and Named Queries in Spring Data JPA. Give One Example of Each.

📝 Topic Focus: 29. Compare derived query methods, @Query, and named queries in Spring Data JPA. Give one example of each.

29. Compare Derived Query Methods, @Query, and Named Queries in Spring Data JPA. Give One Example of Each.

Spring Data JPA provides different methods to retrieve data from a database. Three commonly used approaches are Derived Query Methods, @Query and Named Queries. They differ in how queries are defined and executed.

1. Derived Query Methods

Derived Query Methods are created by writing method names according to predefined naming conventions. Spring Data JPA automatically generates the required query from the method name.

Example:

public interface EmployeeRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Employee, Integer> {

    List<Employee> findByName(String name);
}

Explanation: Spring automatically generates a query to find employees whose name matches the given value.

2. @Query Annotation

The @Query annotation is used to define custom JPQL or native SQL queries directly inside a repository interface. It is useful for complex database operations.

Example:

public interface EmployeeRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Employee, Integer> {

    @Query("SELECT e FROM Employee e WHERE e.salary > :salary")
    List<Employee> findHighSalary(
        @Param("salary") double salary);
}

Explanation: This query retrieves employees whose salary is greater than the given amount.

3. Named Queries

Named Queries are predefined queries identified by a unique name. They are commonly declared using @NamedQuery on an entity class and referenced through a repository method.

Example:

@Entity
@NamedQuery(
    name = "Employee.findAllEmployees",
    query = "SELECT e FROM Employee e"
)
public class Employee {
    @Id
    private int id;
}

Repository method:

List<Employee> findAllEmployees();

Explanation: The repository method uses the predefined named query to retrieve all employees.

4. Comparison

Derived Query @Query Named Query
Based on method names. Uses custom query definitions. Uses predefined named queries.
Simple queries. Simple or complex queries. Reusable predefined queries.
Written in repository methods. Written directly in repository interfaces. Usually defined on entity classes or XML.
Automatically generated. Explicitly written by developer. Defined separately and referenced by name.

Conclusion

Derived Query Methods are suitable for simple queries, @Query is useful for custom queries, and Named Queries are useful for predefined and reusable queries.

Q30. Explain Why Transactions Are Required in Spring Applications. Demonstrate the Use of @Transactional for an Update Operation.

📝 Topic Focus: 30. Explain why transactions are required in Spring applications. Demonstrate the use of @Transactional for an update operation.

30. Explain Why Transactions Are Required in Spring Applications. Demonstrate the Use of @Transactional for an Update Operation.

Transactions in Spring applications are used to ensure that database operations are performed safely and consistently. A transaction is a group of database operations treated as a single unit of work.

Spring provides the @Transactional annotation to manage database transactions automatically.

1. Why Transactions Are Required

  1. Data Consistency: Ensures that database data remains correct after operations.

  2. Atomicity: Either all operations are completed successfully or none of them are applied.

  3. Rollback Support: If an error occurs, changes can be rolled back to maintain database consistency.

  4. Error Handling: Helps manage database failures during multiple operations.

  5. Reliable Updates: Prevents incomplete database updates when an operation fails.

2. ACID Properties

Transactions follow four important ACID properties:

  • Atomicity: All operations succeed or fail together.
  • Consistency: Database remains in a valid state.
  • Isolation: Concurrent transactions do not interfere improperly.
  • Durability: Committed changes are permanently saved.

3. Example Using @Transactional

Suppose we want to update an employee's salary.

Employee Entity:

@Entity
public class Employee {
    @Id
    private int id;
    private double salary;
}

Repository:

public interface EmployeeRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Employee, Integer> {
}

Service Class:

@Service
public class EmployeeService {

    @Autowired
    private EmployeeRepository repository;

    @Transactional
    public void updateSalary(int id, double salary) {

        Employee emp = repository.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow(() ->
                new RuntimeException("Employee not found"));

        emp.setSalary(salary);

        repository.save(emp);
    }
}

4. Explanation

  1. @Transactional starts a transaction when the method is called.
  2. The employee is retrieved using findById().
  3. The salary is updated using setSalary().
  4. save() stores the updated employee.
  5. If the operation completes successfully, the transaction is committed.
  6. If an unchecked exception occurs, the transaction is rolled back by default.

Conclusion

Transactions are required to maintain database consistency and reliability. The @Transactional annotation simplifies transaction management by automatically handling commit and rollback operations.

Q31. Implement Pagination and Sorting for the User Entity Using Pageable and Sort. Explain How the Page Number, Page Size, and Sorting Field Are Specified.

📝 Topic Focus: 31. Implement pagination and sorting for the User entity using Pageable and Sort. Explain how the page number, page size, and sorting field are specified.

31. Implement Pagination and Sorting for the User Entity Using Pageable and Sort. Explain How the Page Number, Page Size, and Sorting Field Are Specified.

Pagination in Spring Data JPA is a technique used to divide a large number of database records into smaller pages. Sorting is used to arrange records in ascending or descending order based on a particular field.

Spring Data JPA provides Pageable, PageRequest and Sort to implement pagination and sorting easily.

1. Repository Interface

public interface UserRepository
        extends JpaRepository<User, Integer> {
}

Here, JpaRepository provides built-in methods for pagination and sorting.

2. Implement Pagination and Sorting

@Service
public class UserService {

    @Autowired
    private UserRepository repository;

    public Page<User> getUsers() {

        Pageable pageable =
            PageRequest.of(0, 5,
                Sort.by("name").ascending());

        return repository.findAll(pageable);
    }
}

3. Explanation

The PageRequest.of() method specifies three important parameters:

  1. Page Number:
  2. Specifies which page should be retrieved.
  3. Page numbering starts from 0.

  4. Example: 0 represents the first page.

  5. Page Size:

  6. Specifies the number of records displayed on each page.

  7. Example: 5 means five user records per page.

  8. Sorting Field:

  9. Specifies the field used to arrange records.
  10. Example: Sort.by("name").ascending() sorts users by name in ascending order.
  11. descending() sorts records in descending order.

4. Example

Pageable pageable = PageRequest.of(
    1, 10, Sort.by("id").descending()
);

Page<User> users = repository.findAll(pageable);

Output: - Page Number: 1 (Second Page) - Page Size: 10 records - Sorting Field: id - Sorting Order: Descending

5. Advantages

  1. Reduces unnecessary data retrieval.
  2. Improves application performance.
  3. Makes large datasets easier to manage.
  4. Supports flexible sorting.

Conclusion

Spring Data JPA uses Pageable, PageRequest and Sort to implement pagination and sorting efficiently. It allows developers to specify the page number, page size and sorting field without writing manual SQL queries.

Q32. What Are Web Services? Explain Why Web Services Are Used in Distributed Applications.

📝 Topic Focus: 32. What are Web Services? Explain why Web Services are used in distributed applications.

32. What Are Web Services? Explain Why Web Services Are Used in Distributed Applications.

Web Services are software components that allow different applications to communicate and exchange data over a network using standard web protocols such as HTTP. They enable applications developed using different programming languages and operating systems to interact with each other.

Web Services are commonly used in distributed applications, where different components run on separate computers or servers but work together to complete a task.

1. Why Web Services Are Used in Distributed Applications

  1. Communication Between Applications: Web Services allow applications running on different systems to communicate and exchange information.

  2. Platform Independence: They support communication between applications developed using different programming languages and operating systems.

  3. Interoperability: They allow different software systems to work together without depending on their internal implementation.

  4. Reusability: The same Web Service can be accessed by multiple applications, reducing repeated development.

  5. Easy Integration: They help connect different systems, databases and applications over a network.

  6. Scalability: Services can be deployed and maintained separately, making it easier to expand distributed applications.

2. Working of Web Services

The basic communication process involves three steps:

  1. Service Provider: Creates and provides the Web Service.
  2. Service Requester: Sends a request to access the service.
  3. Service Response: The provider processes the request and returns the required data.

3. Simple Diagram

🔍 Distributed Web Services Architecture (Client-Provider Request-Response Model) (tap to expand)

4. Example

Consider an online shopping application.

  • The shopping application requests payment processing.
  • The Payment Web Service receives the request.
  • It processes the payment.
  • It sends the payment status back to the shopping application.

Thus, two different applications communicate through a Web Service.

5. Common Types of Web Services

  1. SOAP: Uses XML-based messaging for communication.
  2. REST: Uses HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT and DELETE.

Conclusion

Web Services are important in distributed applications because they provide platform-independent communication, interoperability, reusability and easy integration between different software systems.

1. Create a REST API to Retrieve User Information Using Both @PathVariable and @RequestParam. Test the API Using Postman.

REST API is used to allow applications to communicate with each other through HTTP requests. In Spring Boot, @PathVariable and @RequestParam are used to receive values from client requests and retrieve specific user information.

1. Create User Class

public class User {
    private int id;
    private String name;
    private String email;

    public User(int id, String name, String email) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
        this.email = email;
    }

    public int getId() { return id; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public String getEmail() { return email; }
}

2. Create REST Controller

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

    List<User> users = Arrays.asList(
        new User(1, "Rahul", "rahul@gmail.com"),
        new User(2, "Amit", "amit@gmail.com")
    );

    // Using PathVariable
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public User getUserById(@PathVariable int id) {
        return users.stream()
            .filter(u -> u.getId() == id)
            .findFirst()
            .orElse(null);
    }

    // Using RequestParam
    @GetMapping("/search")
    public User getUserByName(
            @RequestParam String name) {
        return users.stream()
            .filter(u -> u.getName().equalsIgnoreCase(name))
            .findFirst()
            .orElse(null);
    }
}

3. Explanation

@PathVariable: - Extracts values directly from the URL path. - Example: /api/users/1 - Retrieves the user whose ID is 1.

@RequestParam: - Extracts values from URL query parameters. - Example: /api/users/search?name=Rahul - Retrieves the user whose name is Rahul.

4. Test Using Postman

  • Method: GET
  • URL: http://localhost:8080/api/users/1

  "name": "Rahul",

}

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Rahul",

Q34. Explain the Different Types of Web Services. Compare SOAP and REST.

📝 Topic Focus: 34. Explain the different types of Web Services. Compare SOAP and REST.

34. Explain the Different Types of Web Services. Compare SOAP and REST.

Web Services are software components that allow different applications to communicate and exchange data over a network using standard protocols. They help applications developed using different programming languages and platforms interact with each other.

1. Types of Web Services

There are two major types of Web Services:

1. SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol)

  • SOAP is a protocol used for exchanging structured information between applications.
  • It uses XML (Extensible Markup Language) for message formatting.
  • It commonly works over HTTP and supports other transport protocols.
  • It provides standards for security and reliable messaging.
  • Example: Banking and enterprise applications.

2. REST (Representational State Transfer)

  • REST is an architectural style used to develop Web Services.
  • It uses HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT and DELETE.
  • It supports data formats such as JSON and XML.
  • It is lightweight and easy to implement.
  • Example: E-commerce applications and mobile applications.

2. Difference Between SOAP and REST

SOAP REST
1. SOAP is a communication protocol. REST is an architectural style.
2. Uses XML for messages. Supports JSON, XML and other formats.
3. Generally requires more message overhead. Usually has less message overhead.
4. Supports standards such as WS-Security. Commonly uses HTTPS and token-based security.
5. Can work over HTTP, SMTP and other transports. Primarily uses HTTP/HTTPS.
6. Suitable for enterprise and financial systems. Suitable for web and mobile applications.
7. Uses SOAP envelopes for messages. Uses HTTP methods to access resources.

3. Examples

SOAP Request:

<soap:Envelope>
    <soap:Body>
        <getStudent>
            <id>101</id>
        </getStudent>
    </soap:Body>
</soap:Envelope>

REST Request:

GET /api/students/101

4. Applications

  • SOAP: Banking systems, payment processing and enterprise applications.
  • REST: Social media applications, e-commerce websites and mobile applications.

Conclusion

SOAP and REST are two major approaches to building Web Services. SOAP provides a standardized messaging protocol, whereas REST provides a lightweight architectural approach for communication between applications.

Q35. Explain Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) and Its Main Principles.

📝 Topic Focus: 35. Explain Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) and its main principles.

35. Explain Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) and Its Main Principles.

Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) is a software design approach in which an application is divided into independent services. Each service performs a specific business function and communicates with other services over a network.

SOA allows different applications to share services and exchange information without depending on their internal implementation.

1. Main Components of SOA

  1. Service Provider: Creates and provides services to other applications.
  2. Service Consumer: Requests and uses the services provided by another application.
  3. Service Registry: Stores information about available services so consumers can discover them.

2. Main Principles of SOA

1. Loose Coupling - Services have minimal dependency on each other. - Changes in one service have less impact on other services.

2. Reusability - A service can be reused by multiple applications. - It reduces duplicate development work.

3. Standardized Service Contract - Every service provides a defined interface or contract. - Consumers know how to communicate with the service.

4. Service Autonomy - Each service manages its own functionality and resources. - Services can operate independently.

5. Service Discoverability - Services can be identified and accessed through service descriptions or registries.

6. Interoperability - Services developed using different programming languages and platforms can communicate with each other.

3. SOA Architecture Diagram

🔍 Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) Publish-Find-Bind Model (tap to expand)

4. Example

Consider an online shopping application.

  • Payment Service: Processes customer payments.
  • Inventory Service: Checks product availability.
  • Delivery Service: Manages product delivery.
  • Customer Service: Manages customer information.

These independent services communicate with each other to complete an online purchase.

5. Advantages of SOA

  1. Improves service reusability.
  2. Reduces application complexity.
  3. Supports integration of different systems.
  4. Makes applications flexible and scalable.
  5. Simplifies maintenance.

Conclusion

SOA organizes applications into independent and reusable services. Its main principles include loose coupling, reusability, service autonomy, standardized contracts and interoperability.

Q37. Explain the Differences Between `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam`, and `@MatrixVariable` with Suitable Examples.

📝 Topic Focus: 1.      Explain the differences between `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam`, and `@MatrixVariable` with suitable examples.

1. Explain the Differences Between @PathVariable, @RequestParam, and @MatrixVariable with Suitable Examples.

In Spring Boot REST APIs, @PathVariable, @RequestParam and @MatrixVariable are annotations used to extract values from different parts of a URL. They help controllers receive data from client requests.

1. @PathVariable

@PathVariable is used to extract values directly from the URL path.

Example:

@GetMapping("/users/{id}")
public String getUser(@PathVariable int id) {
    return "User ID: " + id;
}

URL:

http://localhost:8080/users/101

Output:

User ID: 101

Here, 101 is extracted from the URL path and assigned to the id variable.

2. @RequestParam

@RequestParam is used to extract values from query parameters in a URL. Query parameters appear after the ? symbol.

Example:

@GetMapping("/users")
public String getUser(
    @RequestParam String name) {
    return "User Name: " + name;
}

URL:

http://localhost:8080/users?name=Rahul

Output:

User Name: Rahul

Here, Rahul is extracted from the query parameter.

3. @MatrixVariable

@MatrixVariable is used to extract key-value pairs from a URL path segment. Matrix variables are separated using semicolons (;).

Example:

@GetMapping("/users/{details}")
public String getUser(
    @MatrixVariable String name) {
    return "User Name: " + name;
}

URL:

http://localhost:8080/users/details;name=Rahul

Output:

User Name: Rahul

Note: Matrix variables must be enabled in Spring MVC configuration when using the default setup.

4. Difference Between Them

Annotation Purpose URL Format
@PathVariable Extracts path values. /users/101
@RequestParam Extracts query parameters. /users?name=Rahul
@MatrixVariable Extracts matrix parameters. /users;name=Rahul

Conclusion

All three annotations extract values from URLs, but their locations are different. @PathVariable extracts path values, @RequestParam extracts query parameters, and @MatrixVariable extracts semicolon-separated matrix parameters.

Q40. Explain Data Validation, Exception Handling, CORS, and Security in Spring REST Applications.

📝 Topic Focus: 40. Explain data validation, exception handling, CORS, and security in Spring REST applications.

40. Explain Data Validation, Exception Handling, CORS, and Security in Spring REST Applications.

Spring REST Applications use different mechanisms to ensure that APIs are reliable, secure and handle client requests properly. Four important concepts are Data Validation, Exception Handling, CORS and Security.

1. Data Validation

Data Validation is the process of checking whether the input data received from clients is correct and valid before processing it.

Spring Boot uses annotations such as:

  • @NotNull – Value must not be null.
  • @NotBlank – String must not be empty or contain only spaces.
  • @Size – Defines minimum and maximum length.
  • @Email – Checks whether the input is a valid email address.

Example:

public class User {
    @NotBlank
    private String name;

    @Email
    private String email;
}

@Valid is used in controller methods to trigger validation.

2. Exception Handling

Exception Handling manages errors that occur during API execution and returns meaningful error responses to clients.

Important annotations:

  • @ExceptionHandler – Handles specific exceptions.
  • @ControllerAdvice – Provides global exception handling.
  • @RestControllerAdvice – Handles exceptions globally and returns response data directly.

Example:

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    public String handleException(Exception ex) {
        return "Something went wrong";
    }
}

3. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)

CORS is a security mechanism that controls whether a web application from one origin can access resources from another origin.

Spring REST uses @CrossOrigin to allow requests from specified origins.

Example:

@CrossOrigin(origins = "http://localhost:3000")
@RestController
public class UserController {
}

Here, requests from the specified frontend origin are allowed, subject to other server security rules.

4. Security

Security protects REST APIs from unauthorized access and ensures that only permitted users can access resources.

Main methods include:

  1. Authentication – Verifies user identity.
  2. Authorization – Controls user permissions.
  3. HTTPS – Encrypts communication.
  4. JWT – Uses tokens for authentication.

Conclusion

Data Validation checks input, Exception Handling manages errors, CORS controls cross-origin access, and Security protects REST APIs from unauthorized access. Together, they make Spring REST applications reliable and secure.

Q41. Create a Spring Boot REST Application for Managing User Resources. Create a UserController and Implement CRUD Operations. Test the APIs Using Postman or curl.

📝 Topic Focus: 41. Create a Spring Boot REST application for managing User resources. Create a UserController and implement CRUD operations. Test the APIs using Postman or curl.

41. Create a Spring Boot REST Application for Managing User Resources. Create a UserController and Implement CRUD Operations. Test the APIs Using Postman or curl.

CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations are used to manage resources in a REST API. Spring Boot provides annotations such as @RestController, @PostMapping, @GetMapping, @PutMapping and @DeleteMapping to implement these operations.

Step 1: Create Spring Boot Project

Open Spring Initializr and select:

  • Project: Maven
  • Language: Java
  • Dependency: Spring Web

Generate and import the project into your IDE.

Step 2: Create User Class

public class User {
    private int id;
    private String name;
    private String email;

    public User(int id, String name, String email) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
        this.email = email;
    }

    public int getId() { return id; }
    public void setId(int id) { this.id = id; }

    public String getName() { return name; }
    public void setName(String name) { this.name = name; }

    public String getEmail() { return email; }
    public void setEmail(String email) { this.email = email; }
}

Step 3: Create UserController

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

    private List<User> users = new ArrayList<>();

    // CREATE
    @PostMapping
    public User addUser(@RequestBody User user) {
        users.add(user);
        return user;
    }

    // READ
    @GetMapping
    public List<User> getUsers() {
        return users;
    }

    // UPDATE
    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public User updateUser(
            @PathVariable int id,
            @RequestBody User updatedUser) {

        for (User user : users) {
            if (user.getId() == id) {
                user.setName(updatedUser.getName());
                user.setEmail(updatedUser.getEmail());
                return user;
            }
        }
        return null;
    }

    // DELETE
    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public String deleteUser(@PathVariable int id) {
        users.removeIf(user -> user.getId() == id);
        return "User deleted successfully";
    }
}

Step 4: Test APIs Using Postman

Operation HTTP Method URL
Create POST /api/users
Read GET /api/users
Update PUT /api/users/1
Delete DELETE /api/users/1

POST Request Body:

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Rahul",
  "email": "rahul@gmail.com"
}

Expected Output:

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Rahul",
  "email": "rahul@gmail.com"
}

Step 5: Test Using curl

curl http://localhost:8080/api/users

Conclusion

This application demonstrates all four CRUD operations using Spring Boot REST APIs. UserController handles client requests and manages User resources through HTTP methods. This example uses an in-memory list; data is not permanently stored in a database.

Q43. Apply Java-Based Configuration Techniques to Set Up and Manage an IoC Container in a Spring Application.

📝 Topic Focus: 43. Apply Java-based configuration techniques to set up and manage an IoC container in a Spring application.

43. Apply Java-Based Configuration Techniques to Set Up and Manage an IoC Container in a Spring Application.

Java-Based Configuration in Spring is a technique used to configure and manage application objects (Spring Beans) using Java classes and annotations instead of XML configuration files.

The IoC (Inversion of Control) Container manages the creation, configuration, dependency injection and lifecycle of Spring Beans.

1. Important Annotations

  1. @Configuration: Indicates that a Java class contains Spring configuration.
  2. @Bean: Defines a method whose returned object is registered as a Spring Bean.
  3. @ComponentScan: Automatically scans packages for Spring components.
  4. @Autowired: Automatically injects required dependencies.

2. Steps to Configure IoC Container

Step 1: Create a Student Class

public class Student {
    public void display() {
        System.out.println("Student Details");
    }
}

Step 2: Create a Configuration Class

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public Student student() {
        return new Student();
    }
}

Here, @Configuration defines the configuration class, and @Bean registers the Student object in the IoC Container.

Step 3: Create the Main Class

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        ApplicationContext context =
            new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(
                AppConfig.class);

        Student s = context.getBean(Student.class);

        s.display();
    }
}

3. Working of IoC Container

  1. The application loads the Java configuration class.
  2. Spring creates the IoC Container.
  3. The container reads the @Bean annotation.
  4. It creates and registers the Student object as a Spring Bean.
  5. getBean() retrieves the required object.
  6. The application uses the retrieved object.

4. Output

Student Details

5. Advantages

  1. Eliminates XML configuration.
  2. Simplifies bean management.
  3. Supports Dependency Injection.
  4. Improves code maintainability.
  5. Provides centralized object management.

Conclusion

Java-Based Configuration helps set up and manage the Spring IoC Container using Java classes and annotations. It simplifies bean creation, configuration and dependency management without requiring XML files.

Q44. Compare Constructor and Setter Injection with Example.

📝 Topic Focus: 44. Compare Constructor and Setter Injection with example

44. Compare Constructor and Setter Injection with Example.

Constructor Injection and Setter Injection are two types of Dependency Injection (DI) in the Spring Framework. They are used to provide required dependencies (objects) to a class. Both help achieve loose coupling between application components.

1. Constructor Injection

Constructor Injection is a technique in which dependencies are provided through the class constructor when an object is created.

Example:

@Component
class Student {
    private final Address address;

    @Autowired
    public Student(Address address) {
        this.address = address;
    }
}

Explanation: - Spring provides the Address object through the constructor. - Dependency is injected during object creation. - It is suitable for mandatory dependencies.

2. Setter Injection

Setter Injection is a technique in which dependencies are provided through setter methods after an object is created.

Example:

@Component
class Student {
    private Address address;

    @Autowired
    public void setAddress(Address address) {
        this.address = address;
    }
}

Explanation: - Spring provides the Address object through the setter method. - Dependency is injected after object creation. - It is suitable for optional dependencies.

3. Difference Between Constructor and Setter Injection

Constructor Injection Setter Injection
1. Uses a constructor to inject dependencies. Uses setter methods to inject dependencies.
2. Dependencies are provided during object creation. Dependencies are provided after object creation.
3. Suitable for mandatory dependencies. Suitable for optional dependencies.
4. Supports immutable fields using final. Dependencies can be changed later.
5. Ensures required dependencies are available during construction. Allows dependencies to be configured later.
6. Generally preferred for required dependencies. Useful for optional dependencies.

4. Advantages

Constructor Injection: - Ensures required dependencies are provided. - Supports immutable objects. - Makes testing easier.

Setter Injection: - Supports optional dependencies. - Allows dependency modification. - Provides flexible configuration.

Conclusion

Constructor Injection is preferred for mandatory dependencies, whereas Setter Injection is suitable for optional dependencies. Both are used by Spring to achieve Dependency Injection and reduce tight coupling between classes.

Q45. Discuss About Dependency Injection (DI).

📝 Topic Focus: 45. Discuss about Dependency Injection?

45. Discuss About Dependency Injection (DI).

Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern in the Spring Framework in which the required objects (dependencies) are provided to a class by the Spring IoC Container instead of the class creating those objects manually.

It is a method of implementing Inversion of Control (IoC). DI helps develop loosely coupled, reusable and maintainable applications.

1. Types of Dependency Injection

Spring supports three main types of Dependency Injection:

1. Constructor Injection - Dependencies are provided through the class constructor. - It is suitable for mandatory dependencies.

Example:

@Component
class Student {
    private final Address address;

    @Autowired
    Student(Address address) {
        this.address = address;
    }
}

2. Setter Injection - Dependencies are provided using setter methods. - It is suitable for optional dependencies.

Example:

@Component
class Student {
    private Address address;

    @Autowired
    public void setAddress(Address address) {
        this.address = address;
    }
}

3. Field Injection - Dependencies are directly injected into class variables. - It uses the @Autowired annotation.

Example:

@Component
class Student {
    @Autowired
    private Address address;
}

2. How Dependency Injection Works

  1. Spring creates the required objects as Spring Beans.
  2. It identifies the dependencies between classes.
  3. The IoC Container searches for the required beans.
  4. It automatically injects the matching objects.
  5. The application uses the injected dependencies.

3. Advantages of Dependency Injection

  1. Loose Coupling: Reduces dependency between classes.
  2. Code Reusability: Allows objects to be reused.
  3. Easy Testing: Makes unit testing easier.
  4. Easy Maintenance: Makes applications easier to modify.
  5. Reduced Code: Avoids manual object creation.

Conclusion

Dependency Injection simplifies object management by allowing Spring to provide required dependencies automatically. It is an important feature of the Spring Framework that helps create flexible and maintainable applications.

Q46. Explain About Auto Scanning in Brief.

📝 Topic Focus: 46. Explain about Auto Scanning in brief

46. Explain About Auto Scanning in Brief.

Auto Scanning in the Spring Framework is a feature that automatically detects classes annotated with Spring annotations and registers them as Spring Beans in the IoC Container.

It uses the @ComponentScan annotation to scan specified packages and identify components. It reduces manual bean configuration and simplifies application development.

1. Annotations Used in Auto Scanning

  1. @Component: Marks a Java class as a Spring-managed component.
  2. @Service: Identifies a class containing business logic.
  3. @Repository: Identifies a class responsible for database operations.
  4. @Controller: Identifies a class that handles web requests.
  5. @RestController: Identifies a class that handles REST API requests.
  6. @ComponentScan: Specifies which packages Spring should scan.

2. Example

Student Class:

@Component
public class Student {
    public void display() {
        System.out.println("Hello Student");
    }
}

Configuration Class:

@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.example")
public class AppConfig {
}

3. How Auto Scanning Works

  1. Developers add annotations such as @Component to Java classes.
  2. @ComponentScan specifies the package to scan.
  3. Spring scans the specified package.
  4. It detects classes containing component annotations.
  5. Spring automatically registers detected classes as Beans.
  6. These Beans can be used through Dependency Injection.

4. Advantages of Auto Scanning

  1. Reduces manual bean configuration.
  2. Simplifies application development.
  3. Supports automatic dependency management.
  4. Improves code organization.
  5. Makes applications easier to maintain.

Conclusion

Auto Scanning automatically detects and registers Spring components as Beans using annotations and @ComponentScan. It reduces manual configuration and simplifies object management in Spring applications.

Q48. Explain the Scope of a Bean and Logger.

📝 Topic Focus: 48. Explain the scope of a bean and Logger?

48. Explain the Scope of a Bean and Logger.

1. Bean Scope in Spring

Bean Scope defines the lifecycle and visibility of a Spring Bean. It determines how many instances of a bean are created and how long they remain available in the Spring IoC Container.

Spring supports six main bean scopes:

  1. Singleton: Only one instance of a bean is created per Spring IoC Container. It is the default scope.

  2. Prototype: A new bean instance is created every time the bean is requested from the container.

  3. Request: A new bean instance is created for each HTTP request.

  4. Session: One bean instance is created for each HTTP session.

  5. Application: One bean instance is created per ServletContext and shared across the web application.

  6. WebSocket: A separate bean instance is created for each WebSocket session.

Example:

@Component
@Scope("prototype")
public class Student {
}

Here, Spring creates a new Student bean whenever it is requested.

2. Logger in Spring Boot

Logger is a tool used to record application activities, events, warnings and errors during program execution.

Spring Boot commonly uses SLF4J as a logging API and Logback as its default logging implementation.

Uses of Logger

  1. Debugging: Helps identify errors in the application.
  2. Monitoring: Tracks application activities.
  3. Error Tracking: Records exceptions and failures.
  4. Information Recording: Displays important application events.

Example of Logger

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

@RestController
public class StudentController {

    private static final Logger logger =
        LoggerFactory.getLogger(StudentController.class);

    @GetMapping("/student")
    public String getStudent() {

        logger.info("Student API called");
        logger.warn("Warning message");
        logger.error("Error occurred");

        return "Student Details";
    }
}

Logging Levels

Level Purpose
TRACE Detailed information
DEBUG Debugging information
INFO Normal application activities
WARN Potential problems
ERROR Serious errors

Conclusion

Bean Scope controls the lifecycle and number of Spring Bean instances, whereas Logger records application activities and errors to help developers monitor and maintain applications.
